opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions right now, because a lot of the jobs where people actually want to deploy AI are exactly the ones where "mostly right" isn't good enough. If you're doing accounting, or medical dosing, or writing code that touches a production database, a 95% success rate can be worse than useless, because now a human has to check everything anyway.

My view is that we probably won't get there just by scaling up the current paradigm of training a big model end to end and hoping reliability emerges. Large language models are amazing at producing plausible outputs, but plausibility and correctness are different things. What you really want for high-precision work is systems that have some explicit representation of what they're trying to achieve, and of the structure of the world they're acting in, so they can reason about it in a way that's checkable.

That's a big part of why I work on what you might call model-based or probabilistic programming approaches. The idea is you combine the flexibility of neural networks, which are great at perception and at proposing hypotheses, with more structured components: explicit models, symbolic constraints, Bayesian inference. Then the system can do things like represent its own uncertainty, notice when it's out of its depth, and verify its outputs against a specification rather than just generating something that looks right.

A concrete example is something like structured generation, constraining what a language model can output so it's guaranteed to satisfy certain rules, or using sequential Monte Carlo to steer generation toward outputs that meet a constraint. You're not hoping the model gets it right; you're building the guarantee into the inference procedure.

The other piece, which I think is underrated, is that precision depends on knowing what the human actually wants. A lot of failures in high-stakes settings aren't failures of capability, they're failures of specification. The system did something that technically satisfied the instruction but missed the intent. So I think we need AI that is genuinely uncertain about people's goals and acts on that uncertainty: asks clarifying questions, defers when stakes are high, infers preferences from context the way a good human assistant would.

So in short: better calibrated uncertainty, more structure and verifiability in how systems reason, and a much richer model of human intentions. I don't think any one of those is sufficient alone, but together they get you much closer to something you'd actually trust with a high-precision job.

r001.rationale: The response says high-precision work needs neural networks combined with structured components such as explicit models, symbolic constraints, and Bayesian inference.

r002.rationale: The response doubts that scaling the current paradigm alone will produce reliable precision, but does not say that achieving the needed precision will take a long time while scaling remains dominant.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at something that's often missing from the current conversation about AI capabilities. When people talk about AI handling high-precision work, whether that's engineering, medicine, law, or scientific research, they often frame it as a matter of scaling up what we already have. Make the models bigger, train on more data, and eventually the error rate drops to acceptable levels. I'm skeptical that's the whole story.

My view is that high precision in these domains isn't primarily about the raw accuracy of individual predictions. It's about having systems that can represent their own uncertainty in a calibrated way, that can reason explicitly about what they know and don't know, and that can defer or ask for clarification when they're outside their competence. A human expert in a high-stakes field isn't someone who never makes mistakes. It's someone who has a very good model of where their mistakes are likely to occur and builds verification procedures around those weak points.

So part of what I think it will take is a shift toward architectures that combine the pattern-recognition strengths of large neural networks with more structured, probabilistic reasoning. A lot of my own work has been on probabilistic programming and Bayesian approaches to inferring goals and intentions, and one of the things that framework gives you is a principled way to maintain and propagate uncertainty. If a system can say, with some reliability, "I'm about eighty percent confident in this step, and the whole chain depends on it," that's enormously more useful in a precision context than a system that outputs a confident answer that happens to be right most of the time.

The second piece is verification and tool use. Many precision tasks have the property that checking an answer is much easier than producing it. You can run the code, you can check the proof, you can simulate the design. Systems that are built to generate candidates and then rigorously verify them, rather than just emitting a final answer, will get to reliability much faster. We're already seeing that in things like formal theorem proving and code generation, where the environment gives hard feedback.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that we need better ways for these systems to understand what the task actually is. A lot of what looks like a precision failure is really a specification failure. The system did something precisely, but it wasn't what the person needed. In high-stakes domains, correctly inferring the intent behind an instruction, including all the implicit norms and constraints that a human would take for granted, is at least as important as executing the instruction flawlessly. That's a problem of modeling human goals and values, not just a problem of accuracy.

So to sum up, I'd say it takes calibrated uncertainty, strong verification loops, and much better models of what people actually want. Scale helps with all three, but I don't think scale alone gets us there.

r001.rationale: The response says high precision will require architectures combining neural networks with structured probabilistic reasoning, alongside uncertainty handling and verification.

r002.rationale: The response doubts that scaling alone is sufficient, but does not clearly say AI will be slow to reach the needed precision while conventional scaling remains dominant.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is being able to check your work. For a task that requires high precision, getting something that looks plausible most of the time isn’t enough. You need ways to verify that the result actually satisfies the constraints of the task.

One promising approach is to combine learning with more explicit reasoning and verification. A model might propose a solution, but then you use tools that can test it, identify mistakes, and feed those mistakes back into the process. That’s particularly useful in domains where correctness can be specified clearly.

The harder case is when the requirements themselves are ambiguous. Then the system also needs to recognize what it doesn’t know, ask for clarification, and know when to defer to a person. So I don’t think it’s just about making models more accurate. It’s about building a process around them that makes errors detectable and recoverable.

r001.rationale: The response says verification is needed and describes combining a model with testing tools, but presents this as one promising approach rather than identifying hybrid systems as necessary.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether AI will achieve the needed precision quickly or whether conventional scaling will remain dominant.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a key distinction is between getting something right most of the time and knowing when you might be wrong. For high-precision work, you need both competence and a reliable way to check the result.

That might mean combining a model with tools that impose stronger constraints. If you're writing software, you can run tests or, in some cases, formally verify properties of the program. If you're making a plan, you can check whether it satisfies the relevant constraints before executing it. The model doesn't have to do everything in a single shot.

The harder cases are where checking is itself difficult, or where the task is underspecified. Then the system needs to recognize uncertainty, ask for clarification, and defer to a person when appropriate. So I suspect progress will come from building systems that can reason, check, and revise their work, alongside improving the underlying models.

r001.rationale: The response says high-precision work needs both model competence and reliable checking, and describes combining a model with tools that enforce constraints.

r002.rationale: The response does not express doubt about rapid progress or say that conventional scaling remains the dominant approach.
